Female Hokkaido sculpin attain a maximum body length of 15 centimeters [Li = 15 centimeters], a value that represents the upper limit of somatic growth observed in this species. This ultimate total length is notably modest compared to larger-bodied cottids occupying deeper river systems across the Japanese archipelago. Reproduction in Cottus hangiongensis has been studied under controlled laboratory conditions, providing key insights into its life history strategy. When maintained at a stable water temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C], females produce approximately 500 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 500 eggs per spawning event] over the course of a year [F_R_i = over the course of a year]. This rate reflects a combination of clutch size and spawning frequency that allows the species to persist in the fast-flowing, cool streams of Hokkaido. The relatively high reproductive output is likely an adaptation to elevated rates of early-life mortality experienced by the pelagic larva. Comparative data from other freshwater sculpins suggest that this level of fecundity is consistent with a strategy prioritizing numerical offspring production over per-offspring investment. The thermal regime of 13 °C is typical of the natal streams inhabited by this species during the spring spawning period.

Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae of the Hokkaido sculpin emerge from demersal eggs at a remarkably small size, weighing only 0.0048 grams [Wwb = 0.0048 grams] at birth. This minimal wet weight reflects the limited yolk reserves available to the lecithotrophic larva during its brief endotrophic phase prior to first exogenous feeding. The tiny mass at eclosion places Cottus hangiongensis among the smaller-bodied freshwater cottids in terms of neonatal investment, a trait that is often linked to the production of numerous, small eggs. Following hatching, the prolarvae must rapidly develop functional mouthparts and digestive capabilities to begin capturing prey, as the endogenous yolk supply is depleted quickly. The transition to active feeding is a critical bottleneck; individuals that fail to locate suitable microzooplankton within a narrow temporal window may reach their point of no return. This high-risk early life stage is partially offset by the substantial numbers of eggs produced each spawning season. The small birth mass of 0.0048 grams [Wwb = 0.0048 grams] therefore represents a trade-off between fecundity and offspring size that is common among iteroparous freshwater fishes inhabiting unpredictable environments.

The total length at which female Hokkaido sculpin first attain sexual maturity is 5.2 centimeters [Lp = 5.2 centimeters], a size typically reached during their second year of growth. This threshold for puberty marks the initiation of gonadal recrudescence and the onset of vitellogenesis in females. Field surveys of stream-dwelling populations indicate that individuals below this length consistently display immature gonads, while those exceeding it show progressive oocyte development. The relatively small size at maturity compared to the ultimate total length of 15 centimeters [Li = 15 centimeters] suggests that Cottus hangiongensis allocates resources to reproduction early in its lifespan, a pattern common among short-lived freshwater fishes. Reaching puberty at 5.2 centimeters [Lp = 5.2 centimeters] total length allows females to participate in multiple spawning seasons, thereby enhancing lifetime reproductive success. This size-based maturity schedule is influenced by local environmental conditions, particularly water temperature and food availability, which can accelerate or delay the attainment of the critical length. Data from mark-recapture studies confirm that most females spawn for the first time in their second spring, having accumulated sufficient somatic reserves during the preceding summer and autumn.

Females that have completed somatic growth attain an ultimate wet weight of 21.7 grams [Wwi = 21.7 grams], with this adult body mass corresponding to the structural length ceiling of 15 centimeters [Li = 15 centimeters] typical of the species. This adult body mass is achieved through a period of rapid mass gain during the juvenile stage, after which growth plateaus as resources are increasingly diverted toward gamete production. Gravid females approaching this weight are capable of carrying large clutches, contributing to the species' moderately high daily reproductive output under optimal thermal conditions. The accumulation of body mass to the ultimate wet weight of 21.7 grams [Wwi = 21.7 grams] is energetically demanding, requiring sustained high feeding rates on benthic macroinvertebrates. Seasonal variation in prey abundance can result in inter-annual differences in the proportion of females attaining this maximum size. Comparisons with similar-sized cottids show that this asymptotic mass supports a fecundity regime that balances current reproductive effort against the need for somatic maintenance and future breeding opportunities in an iteroparous lifecycle.

Maximum longevity in the Hokkaido sculpin has been documented at 8 years [am = 8 years] when individuals are reared under a constant temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C] in captive settings. This lifespan of 8 years [am = 8 years] places Cottus hangiongensis among the longer-lived members of its genus, with many congeneric species exhibiting maximum ages of only 4 to 6 years at a temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. The extended lifespan may be linked to the cool, well-oxygenated waters of Hokkaido streams, which reduce metabolic rates and slow the accumulation of oxidative damage. Reproductively active adults can participate in multiple spawning seasons across their lives, with senescence and age-related death typically occurring in the post-reproductive period after the eighth year. Natural mortality in the wild is likely higher than observed in captivity due to predation and environmental stochasticity, but the species' iteroparous strategy ensures that even with some mortality, a portion of the population survives to reproduce in subsequent years. The longevity of 8 years [am = 8 years] also allows for delayed reproduction in unfavorable years, providing a demographic buffer at a temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. This life history pattern is consistent with that of a cold-adapted freshwater sculpin investing gradually in reproduction over an extended adult phase.
